title: Where Does Shilajit Come From? The People Behind It
description: Where does Shilajit come from? Inside the Himalayan rock, the collectors who climb for it, and the mountain communities whose knowledge made it known.
bodyHtml:
Ask most people where Shilajit comes from and you will get a one-word answer: the Himalayas. It is true, and it tells you almost nothing. The Himalayas span five countries and 2,400 kilometres. The more honest answer involves specific rock faces at specific altitudes, and, far more importantly, the people who know where to find them. We started Salxir because of those people, and this article is our attempt to say so properly.

What Shilajit actually is, geologically

Shilajit is not a plant, a mineral, or an animal product. It is what remains after layers of alpine plant matter are compressed inside rock over an extraordinarily long period, slowly altered by microbial activity, pressure and cold. In the warmer months, the resin softens and seeps out through cracks in the rock as a dark, tar-like exudate.

It forms in a narrow band of conditions. Generally high altitude, in the 1,000 to 5,000 metre range, where the rock, the cold and the plant history all line up. That is why it appears across the Himalaya, Karakoram, Hindu Kush, Altai, Caucasus and a handful of other ranges, and essentially nowhere else. Our fuller explainer covers the chemistry in more depth: what is Shilajit.

Somebody has to climb up and get it

This is the part the marketing usually skips. Shilajit cannot be farmed. It cannot be harvested at scale by machine. Every gram of genuine resin was collected by a person who walked to a remote rock face at altitude, often several days from the nearest road, and scraped it out by hand.

The collectors are typically from mountain communities who have done this for generations, and the knowledge involved is not trivial. Which faces produce good material and which do not. What time of year the seep runs. How to tell the real exudate from the mineral waxes that look almost identical to an untrained eye. It is the same problem consumers face when sorting real from fake Shilajit, except they solve it by touch and smell at 4,000 metres.

It is genuinely dangerous work, done for a fraction of what the finished jar sells for in Europe. Any brand that talks about "ancient Himalayan wisdom" without acknowledging that it is also present-tense Himalayan labour is telling you half a story.

The mountain communities, and what we can honestly claim

Here is where we want to be careful, because this is where the supplement industry tends to lose its grip on the facts.

Shilajit has a long documented history in Ayurvedic and Tibetan medical traditions, where it appears under names including silajatu and brag zhun. This is not vague folklore. Brag zhun is recorded in the Somaratsa, a Tibetan medical text compiled in the mid eighth century, and it sits in the Tibetan materia medica as a restorative associated with the lungs and kidneys and with fatigue and weakness.

That lineage runs directly through Sherpa communities. Sherpas are a Tibetan descended people, and their traditional medical system is Sowa Rigpa, the amchi tradition, which is still practised in Solukhumbu today. So when people say Shilajit has been used in Sherpa communities for a very long time, that is a fair claim with real documentation behind it, not something a marketing team invented.

Where it goes wrong is the next step. You will read on a great many websites that Sherpas eat Shilajit daily and that this is why they can carry loads at altitudes that flatten everyone else. That specific causal claim is not what the evidence supports. Sherpa high altitude performance is one of the better studied cases of human adaptation in the scientific literature, and it is largely genetic, involving variants around genes such as EPAS1 and EGLN1 that change how their bodies handle low oxygen. That is inherited over millennia, not something you can buy in a jar.

Both things are true at once, and we think the honest version is more interesting than either half on its own. The tradition is real and deserves respect. It is just not the explanation for their physiology, and we would rather say that plainly than borrow someone else's biology to sell a product.

What the research does offer is modest and ongoing. A frequently cited paper in the International Journal of Ayurveda Research, "Shilajit: A Panacea for High-Altitude Problems," reviewed traditional altitude use and proposed mechanisms, but it is a review, largely within the Ayurvedic literature, not a settled clinical case. Fulvic acid and trace mineral content are measurable and real. The rest is a field still being worked out.

Why this became a company

Salxir exists because the gap between those two ends of the chain bothered us. On one side, mountain communities holding centuries of specific, hard-won knowledge, doing physically dangerous work, capturing very little of the value. On the other: a European market full of jars with a mountain on the label, no batch number, no lab report, and no traceable origin at all.

We could not fix all of that. What we could do was run the chain properly at our end. Source with traceability rather than vagueness, lab-test every batch for heavy metals and fulvic acid content, handle and pack it here in Finland under Finnish Food Authority oversight, and publish what we find rather than what sells best. When we say #WithLoveFromEarth, the Earth in question has an address, and people living at it.

What to ask any Shilajit brand

If you take one practical thing from this: origin specificity is a quality signal. A brand that can tell you the region, the processing method, and show you a recent third-party Certificate of Analysis tied to your batch number is a brand with an actual supply chain. "Sourced from the Himalayas" with nothing behind it is a stock photo.

Our Himalayan Shilajit resin is the closest thing to what comes off the rock, purified and tested batch by batch, or you can see the full range if a capsule or honey stick suits your routine better. Either way, ask us the hard questions. We would rather answer them than have you take our word for it.
